A 16-session course, from a raw CSV to a deployed model

Author

Author

Published

September 24, 2026

Note

This is a book you read alone. Every idea is explained from the beginning, every term is defined the first time it appears, and every piece of code on these pages actually ran when the book was built. The numbers you see are the numbers the code produced.

Every demonstration loads a real file. Nothing is typed into the program as a Python list, because that is not how data arrives. The files live in datasets/ and are read the way a real project reads them:

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/messy_customers.csv")

0.2 Who this is for

Anyone who wants to work with data and has no prior background in statistics, machine learning, or Python. Session 1 assumes you can use a computer. Nothing else.

0.3 How the course is built

Sixteen sessions in five parts. Each part exists because the one before it is not enough on its own.

Part Sessions The question it answers
A — Getting hold of data 1–2 What is this field, and how do I load a dataset?
B — Making data fit to use 3–6 It is messy, scattered and too wide. Now what?
C — Understanding data 7–8 What is actually in here?
D — Learning from data 9–12 What can be predicted, is it real, and how do others use it?
E — Data at scale 13–16 What changes when it no longer fits on one machine?

0.4 The sessions

# Session You will be able to
1 Introduction to Data Science Name the seven lifecycle stages and place AI, ML and GenAI correctly
2 Data Collection and Pre-Processing Load from CSV, JSON and SQL; select, filter and group
3 Data Cleaning Run the six cleaning jobs in the order that does not hide errors
4 Data Integration Join tables and detect a join that lost or multiplied rows
5 Data Transformation Split before you scale, encode text, and avoid leakage
6 Data Reduction and Discretization Cut columns without cutting the signal
7 Descriptive Statistics Report centre, spread and shape honestly
8 EDA and Visualization Pick the chart that answers the question you asked
9 Supervised Learning Fit a regression, interpret it, and beat a baseline
10 Unsupervised Learning and Clustering Choose k and defend it
11 Model Evaluation Cross-validate, diagnose, and tune without cheating
12 Model Saving and Deployment Ship a working prediction app
13 Big Data Fundamentals Measure where your own machine stops coping
14 Distributed Data Processing Trace map, shuffle and reduce, and read PySpark
15 NoSQL and Visualization at Scale Write an aggregation pipeline and plot ten million rows
16 Capstone Deliver and defend a complete project

0.5 How each session is written

Every session follows the same shape, so once you have read two you can predict the third.

Element What it is
Demo runnable code that demonstrates one idea. Most sessions have eight to fifteen.
🧠 Analogy an everyday comparison — used only where a concept genuinely needs one
⚠️ Trap a mistake that produces a wrong answer without raising an error
🔓 Key idea something you must carry into later sessions
❓ Check yourself short questions with worked answers, folded away
✏️ Tasks things to do, with solutions folded away
✅ Before you move on the checklist for that session
Tip🧠 What makes this course different

Nothing here is asserted without being measured. Where a demonstration contradicted the lesson it was written for, the lesson was changed and the number kept. You will find, among other things:

  • 80% accuracy manufactured from coin flips, by one careless line
  • a model saved without its scaler, valuing a flat at ₹1.69 billion instead of ₹5 million
  • a polynomial that fits its training data best and scores −187 on new data
  • a “best” model chosen by peeking, reported at +0.08 and worth −0.20 in truth
  • K-Means confidently finding three clusters in pure random noise

Those are the passages that teach the most, because they are what you will actually meet.

0.6 The data

Eight of the datasets are real published files — a car marketplace, a loan book, mall customers, heart-failure patients. The rest are generated by a seeded script in the datasets/ folder, and only where a chapter needs a property no real file has: a known cluster structure, a planted association rule, a deliberate leak.

Rebuild every generated file python datasets/make_all.py
Re-download the real ones python datasets/download_real.py
Get the two large real datasets for Sessions 13–14 python datasets/download_bigdata_real.py
What each file is for datasets/README.md

The formats vary on purpose — CSV, JSON, plain text, Excel, SQL, and one table split across several files — because real data does not arrive in one shape.

Sessions 13 and 14 each close with an advanced demo on a genuinely large public dataset — 566,602 real rows of US Forest Service terrain data, and 25,000 real IMDB movie reviews, both from Hugging Face — so the chunking and MapReduce ideas are proven at real scale, not just on data built for the lesson.

0.7 Slides

A companion slide deck covers every session’s concepts — no code, one section per session — for teaching from the front of a room: slides/data-science-course.tex (compile with latexmk -xelatex data-science-course.tex; the built PDF sits alongside it).

0.8 Setting up

All code runs in one conda environment. Create it once:

conda create -n ds python=3.11 -y
conda activate ds
pip install -r requirements.txt

Then build the book with quarto render, or open any session and run the cells in Jupyter. Every session is self-contained — variables do not carry from one to the next, so you can start anywhere, though the order is designed to be read straight through.

0.9 A note on the order

Sessions 3–6 prepare data; Sessions 7–8 describe it. If you have met this material before you may expect statistics to come first — it is the more common arrangement.

Session 3 borrows the two ideas it needs (quartiles and standard deviation) in a marked box, so nothing is used before it is explained, and Session 7 then covers them properly. If you prefer, read Sessions 7 and 8 before Session 3. Nothing in them depends on Sessions 3–6.
